items.title: 1.7 Complex Numbers in the Real World (Voltage, Current and Resistance)

source_refs.note: Book pp. 19-20: printed heading "1.5 Complex Numbers in the Real World" (number repeated), Ohm's law, impedance triangle, Example 17, Cryptography, Example 18 and its table (stops before Exercise 1.5)

blocks.text: 1.5 Complex Numbers in the Real World (Voltage, Current and Resistance)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints this heading as 1.5, a number it already used for "Four Fourth Roots of Unity" (book page 12). We keep the printed number so you can find it in your textbook; only the numbering is wrong.

Ohm's Law is a fundamental principle of physics that describes the relationship between voltage \(V\), current \(I\) and resistance \(R\) in an electrical circuit:
\[V = IR\]

When dealing with alternating current (AC) circuits, resistance generalizes to impedance \(Z\). The book says: Resistance in a circuit is due to inductor \((X_L)\) and capacitor \((X_C)\). Their difference is the reactance
\[X = X_L - X_C\]
Geometrically this is shown in the adjacent figure. Here
\[Z = R + iX\]
Then, for AC circuits, Ohm's Law in terms of impedance is
\[V = I \cdot Z\]
book_errors: Resistance in a circuit is due to inductor

blocks.alt: Right triangle with the right angle at the bottom right: horizontal base R, vertical side labelled X = (X_L) minus (X_C), and the slanting side Z.
blocks.caption: Figure: the impedance triangle, Z = R + iX (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says "Resistance in a circuit is due to inductor \((X_L)\) and capacitor \((X_C)\)". The opposition caused by the inductor and the capacitor is called reactance (\(X_L\) and \(X_C\)), not resistance. Resistance \(R\) comes from resistors and wires. Impedance \(Z = R + iX\) combines both, exactly as the book's figure shows.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why do complex numbers appear here? In an AC circuit the effect of the resistance and the effect of the reactance are a quarter-cycle (90°) apart, just like the real and imaginary axes are at right angles. So we put the resistance on the real axis and the reactance on the imaginary axis: \(Z = R + iX\).
• The size of the total opposition is the modulus \(|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + X^2}\) (Pythagoras in the triangle).
• Its angle is \(\tan^{-1}(X/R)\).
• In polar form, \(Z = |Z|(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi)\), and \(V = IZ\) becomes a multiplication, \(I = V/Z\) a division: exactly the polar rules of 1.3.3.
Engineers usually write \(j\) instead of \(i\), because \(I\) (or \(i\)) is already used for current.

blocks.title: Example 17
blocks.problem: If the impedance of circuit is \(11(\cos 55.35^{\circ} + i\sin 55.35^{\circ})\) ohms at a voltage of \(25(\cos 30^{\circ} + i\sin 30^{\circ})\) V, find the value of current in the circuit.
steps:
Given: impedance \(Z = 11(\cos 55.35^{\circ} + i\sin 55.35^{\circ})\) ohms, voltage \(V = 25(\cos 30^{\circ} + i\sin 30^{\circ})\) volts.
To find: the current \(I\).
Method: Ohm's law for AC, \(V = IZ\), gives \(I = V/Z\). Both are in polar form, so divide the moduli and subtract the arguments (1.3.3).

Substitute in V = IZ
\[25(\cos 30^{\circ} + i\sin 30^{\circ})\]
\[= I \cdot 11(\cos 55.35^{\circ} + i\sin 55.35^{\circ})\]
\[I = \dfrac{V}{Z}\]
Why: divide both sides by \(Z\) to make \(I\) the subject.

Divide in polar form
\[|I| = \dfrac{25}{11} \approx 2.2727\]
\[\theta = 30^{\circ} - 55.35^{\circ} = -25.35^{\circ}\]
\[I = 2.27[\cos(-25.35^{\circ}) + i\sin(-25.35^{\circ})]\]
Why: quotient rule, \(\frac{r_1}{r_2}[\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2) + i\sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2)]\). Keep \(25/11 = 2.2727...\) unrounded for the next step.

Find the cosine and sine
\[\cos(-25.35^{\circ}) = \cos 25.35^{\circ} \approx 0.9037\]
\[\sin(-25.35^{\circ}) = -\sin 25.35^{\circ} \approx -0.4281\]
Why: cosine is even, \(\cos(-A) = \cos A\); sine is odd, \(\sin(-A) = -\sin A\). Use a calculator in degree mode.

Express in rectangular form
\[\text{Re} = 2.2727 \times 0.9037 \approx 2.054\]
\[\text{Im} = 2.2727 \times (-0.4281) \approx -0.973\]
\[I \approx 2.05 - 0.97i\]
Why: \(r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r\cos\theta + i\,r\sin\theta\). The book rounds early (\(2.27 \times 0.90\) and \(2.27 \times 0.42\)) and gets \(2.04 - 0.95i\), which is wrong in the second decimal place.

The book's final line
The book ends with "Thus, current is \(6 - 4.21i\)". This contradicts its own working just above it; the current is \(I \approx 2.05 - 0.97i\) (see the Book correction below).

Check
Multiply back: \(|I| \cdot |Z| = 2.2727 \times 11 = 25\) and \(-25.35^{\circ} + 55.35^{\circ} = 30^{\circ}\), so \(IZ = 25(\cos 30^{\circ} + i\sin 30^{\circ}) = V\).
In rectangular form: \(Z \approx 6.254 + 9.049i\) and
\[(2.054 - 0.973i)(6.254 + 9.049i)\]
\[\approx 21.65 + 12.50i\]
which is \(25\cos 30^{\circ} + i\,25\sin 30^{\circ}\). Correct.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
Example 17: the book's last line prints "Thus, current is \(6 - 4.21i\)", which does not follow from its own working. Its previous line, \(2.04 - 0.95i\), is also slightly off because \(2.27\), \(0.90\) and \(0.42\) were rounded too early. With \(25/11 = 2.2727\), \(\cos 25.35^{\circ} = 0.9037\) and \(\sin 25.35^{\circ} = 0.4281\), the current is
\[I \approx 2.05 - 0.97i \text{ A}\]
(modulus \(2.27\) A, angle \(-25.35^{\circ}\)).
The book's solution also prints a capital "I" inside \(\cos 30^{\circ} + I\sin 30^{\circ}\) and \(\cos 55.35^{\circ} + I\sin 55.35^{\circ}\); there it means \(i\) (iota), not the current.

blocks.title: Example 18
blocks.problem:
The word "MATH" is to be encrypted by multiplying a complex number \(k = 2 + 3i\) and then decrypted back to its original form using the concept of multiplicative inverse in complex numbers.
Each letter of the alphabet is assigned a numerical value as follows: A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, ..., Z = 26.
steps:
Given: the word MATH, the letter values A = 1, ..., Z = 26, and the key \(k = 2 + 3i\).
To find: the encrypted numbers, and show that decryption gives MATH back.
Method: encryption is multiplication by \(k\); decryption is division by \(k\), i.e. multiplication by the multiplicative inverse \(k^{-1}\).

Turn the letters into complex numbers
M = 13, A = 1, T = 20, H = 8, so
\[z = 13 + 0i,\ 1 + 0i,\ 20 + 0i,\ 8 + 0i\]
Why: each letter becomes a complex number with zero imaginary part, so we can multiply it by a complex key.

Encrypt: multiply by k
\[(13 + 0i)(2 + 3i) = 26 + 39i\]
\[(1 + 0i)(2 + 3i) = 2 + 3i\]
\[(20 + 0i)(2 + 3i) = 40 + 60i\]
\[(8 + 0i)(2 + 3i) = 16 + 24i\]
Why: a real number \(n\) times \(2 + 3i\) is \(2n + 3ni\); both parts are multiplied by \(n\).

Find the multiplicative inverse of k
\[k^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2 + 3i} \cdot \dfrac{2 - 3i}{2 - 3i}\]
\[= \dfrac{2 - 3i}{4 + 9} = \dfrac{2 - 3i}{13}\]
Why: \(k \cdot k^{-1} = 1\); multiplying by the conjugate makes the denominator real, \((2 + 3i)(2 - 3i) = 4 - 9i^2 = 13\).

Decrypt A, T, H
Each encrypted number is a real multiple of \(2 + 3i\):
\[2 + 3i = 1(2 + 3i) \Rightarrow 1 = \text{A}\]
\[40 + 60i = 20(2 + 3i) \Rightarrow 20 = \text{T}\]
\[16 + 24i = 8(2 + 3i) \Rightarrow 8 = \text{H}\]
Why: \(\dfrac{n(2 + 3i)}{2 + 3i} = n\).

Check
Decrypted values \(13, 1, 20, 8\) give the letters M, A, T, H: the original word. The book's table below shows the same results.
blocks.answer: Encrypted: M \(\to 26 + 39i\), A \(\to 2 + 3i\), T \(\to 40 + 60i\), H \(\to 16 + 24i\). Dividing each by \(k = 2 + 3i\) gives back \(13, 1, 20, 8\) = MATH.

blocks.caption: Table (as printed in the book): encryption and decryption of MATH with k = 2 + 3i

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
In the table, the rows for T and H leave out the brackets round the key: the book prints \((40 + 60i) / 2 + 3i = 20 + 0i\) and \(16 + 24i / 2 + 3i = 8 + 0i\). Read literally, \((40 + 60i)/2 + 3i\) would be \(20 + 33i\). They should be
\[\dfrac{40 + 60i}{2 + 3i} = 20 + 0i\]
\[\dfrac{16 + 24i}{2 + 3i} = 8 + 0i\]
All the numbers in the table are otherwise correct.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does this work? Multiplying by \(k\) and then dividing by \(k\) undoes itself, because \(k \cdot k^{-1} = 1\). That is why the key must not be \(0\): \(0\) has no multiplicative inverse.
Someone who sees only \(26 + 39i, 2 + 3i, \ldots\) cannot read the word without knowing \(k\). Real cryptography uses much stronger mathematics, but the idea of a key and its inverse is the same.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
• DC: \(V = IR\). AC: \(V = IZ\) with impedance \(Z = R + iX\), reactance \(X = X_L - X_C\).
• \(|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + X^2}\) is the total opposition; in polar form \(I = V/Z\) is a polar division.
• Keep full calculator values until the last step; round only the final answer.
• Encryption here: multiply by \(k\). Decryption: divide by \(k\) (multiply by \(k^{-1} = \overline{k}/|k|^2\)).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
• Subtracting the angles the wrong way: \(I = V/Z\) has angle \(\theta_V - \theta_Z = 30^{\circ} - 55.35^{\circ}\), not \(55.35^{\circ} - 30^{\circ}\).
• Rounding \(25/11\), \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) to two figures before multiplying: the second decimal of the answer goes wrong.
• Calculator in radian mode while the angles are in degrees.
• Writing \(a + bi / c + di\) without brackets; it must be \((a + bi)/(c + di)\).
